plan.topic: Orforglipron gets an EU green light: how is this GLP-1 pill different?
plan.angle: Answer by 10 s: 'It's a small-molecule pill, not a peptide. Its US label says you can take it any time of day without food or water rules.' ATTAIN-1: 12.4% average weight loss on the highest trial dose vs 0.9% on placebo over 72 weeks, in adults with obesity or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes (group sizes in narration). Status line: 'EU medicines committee recommended approval Oct 15, 2026 (published Oct 16); final European Commission decision pending; US-approved for weight management Apr 1, 2026.' Side effects line: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea. 'Follow for more.' Prescriber line.

plan.why: Spin-off of L1. It brings the breaking CHMP news into a Short, and pill explainers have done well on both YouTube and Instagram (55 and 52). | fact-check: Facts check out with corrections. The CHMP opinion was adopted Oct 15, 2026 and published Oct 16 (https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/medicines/human/EPAR/foundayo). EMA's summary of opinion does not mention food or water. That claim comes from the US label and Lilly (https://www.biospace.com/press-releases/fda-approves-lillys-foundayo-orforglipron-the-only-glp-1-pill-for-weight-loss-that-can-be-taken-any-time-of-day-without-food-or-water-restrictions), so 'per EMA' must go. The EU recommendation covers obesity/overweight AND type 2 diabetes. ATTAIN-1 number to use: 12.4% average weight loss on the highest dose (36 mg) vs 0.9% on placebo at 72 weeks, in adults with obesity or overweight with a weight-related condition, without diabetes. Confirm the figure and group sizes against NEJM. Say 'highest dose in the trial' rather than naming mg, to avoid implying a marketed strength or dose. Title 'Gets EU Backing' is fine. Never write 'EU approved' or 'green light' on screen without 'recommended'. Side effects line: mostly stomach-related (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea) per EMA.

package.title: Orforglipron: EU Committee Backs This Pill — What's Different? #shorts
package.description:
An EU committee recommended orforglipron, a small-molecule GLP-1 pill, for approval Oct 15, 2026 (European Commission decision pending); it's already FDA-approved for weight management (Apr 1, 2026). In the 72-week ATTAIN-1 trial (adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes), the highest-dose group lost 12.4% of body weight on average vs 0.9% on placebo among those who stayed on treatment, or 11.2% vs 2.1% counting everyone — Lilly reported. Side effects were mostly stomach-related and mild to moderate.

This content is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always talk to a qualified healthcare professional about your own situation. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

Sources:
- CHMP summary of opinion on Foundayo (orforglipron), adopted Oct 15, 2026, updated Oct 16, 2026 — European Medicines Agency, 2026. https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/medicines/human/EPAR/foundayo
- Orforglipron, an Oral Small-Molecule GLP-1 Receptor Agonist for Obesity Treatment — NEJM, 2025. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40960239/

factcheck.summary:
I checked every claim in this Short against a primary or official source, and all of them hold up.

**Trial numbers (ATTAIN-1, NEJM, PMID 40960239):**
- Population: 3,127 adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes. 72 weeks.
- Group sizes: 730 on 36 mg vs 949 on placebo, so "about 730" and "about 950" are right.
- Counting everyone (the treatment-regimen result): 11.2% vs 2.1%.
- People who stayed on treatment: 12.4% vs 0.9%. Lilly reported this in its FDA approval release, so "Lilly reported" is credited correctly.
- Side effects: NEJM says the most common were gastrointestinal and mostly mild to moderate.

**EMA page:**
- The EU medicines committee (CHMP) gave a positive opinion on Oct 15, 2026. The page was last updated Oct 16.
- Indications: weight management (BMI ≥30, or ≥27 with a weight-related condition) and type 2 diabetes.
- The most common side effects listed are nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea.
- The European Commission hasn't decided yet, so "hasn't decided yet" is correct.

**Lilly release (Apr 1, 2026):**
- FDA approval for chronic weight management in adults with obesity, or overweight with a weight-related condition.
- Small-molecule, not a peptide.
- Taken any time of day, no food or water restrictions.

**Safety and framing:** The prescriber line is there. There's no dosing advice ("highest dose in the trial" isn't an instruction), no sourcing or buying information, both estimands are shown, and the hedges are fine.

**Minor fixes only:**
- The on-screen stat in s4 shows only the higher number.
- The NEJM date should say it's the online publication date.
- The title wording "EU backing" could be clearer.
- The Lilly URL returned 403 to my fetch tool, but search confirms it's the canonical release and it's indexed, so I kept it.

issues.claim: 12.4% vs 0.9% placebo, if stayed on treatment
issues.problem: The screen shows only the more favourable result (people who stayed on treatment). The narration also gives the count-everyone result (11.2% vs 2.1%). The screen shouldn't look more favourable than the narration.
issues.fix: Replace the on-screen text with: "Stayed on treatment: 12.4% vs 0.9% · Everyone: 11.2% vs 2.1%". Keep each figure whole on one caption card.

issues.problem: Sept 16, 2025 is the online-first date. The print issue is NEJM 2025;393(18):1796-1806, dated Nov 6, 2025. Without a label, the date is ambiguous.
issues.fix: Change the title to: "Orforglipron, an Oral Small-Molecule GLP-1 Receptor Agonist for Obesity Treatment (NEJM, published online Sept 16, 2025; N Engl J Med 2025;393:1796-1806)"

issues.problem: "EU backing" is accurate for a committee recommendation, but some viewers may read it as full EU approval. The Commission's decision is still pending.
issues.fix: Optionally change the title to: "Orforglipron Pill Backed by EU Committee: How Is It Different? #shorts"

issues.claim: Its US label says take it any time of day, no food or water rules.
issues.problem: The cited source is Lilly's FDA approval release, not the label itself. The release does state this, so the claim is supported. The attribution is just slightly loose.
issues.fix: Optionally change to: "In the US, it's approved to be taken any time of day, with no food or water rules." Alternatively, keep the wording as it is; the claim is supported.
